01.note: Rabbi Ḥiyya and Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi were debating whether one who prays should look down or up, each citing a verse. Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei, joined them and quoted his father: eyes down, heart up. When Rabbi entered the study hall, the heavy Rabbi Yishmael stepped over the heads of those seated, and Rabbi's attendant Abdon challenged him; the exchange ended with Yishmael asking, 'Is your teacher God?' When a yevama came, Rabbi sent Abdon to examine her, but Yishmael quoted his father that a minor may perform ḥalitza, so Rabbi called Abdon back. Yishmael rebuked him for stepping over heads again, and Rabbi told Abdon to stay where he was. At that moment Abdon was struck with leprosy, his two sons drowned, and their wives refused their marriages.
01.why: The Gemara asks who the Rabbis are who, against Rabbi Meir, let a female minor perform ḥalitza, and answers that it is Rabbi Yosei, as his son reports him in this incident.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya
people.about: Sits debating the direction of one's gaze in prayer with Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei
people.about: A very heavy Sage who quotes his father's rulings and clashes with Abdon.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, head of the study hall; Abdon is his student and attendant.

people.name: Abdon
people.about: Rabbi's student and attendant, who challenges Rabbi Yishmael and is then punished.

people.name: Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak
people.about: Comments that God shamed Abdon in this world, sparing him in the World-to-Come.

terms.meaning: The ceremony in which a childless widow removes the shoe of her late husband's brother, releasing both from the duty of levirate marriage so she may marry someone else.
A childless widow bound to her late husband's brother under the law of levirate marriage until he marries her or performs ḥalitza.
A girl married off as a minor could annul the marriage by declaring that she refuses her husband.

02.note: A widow was bound to her late husband's brother, but he was not suitable for her. The judges told him to let her perform ḥalitza on condition that she pay him two hundred dinars. The case later came before Rabbi Ḥiyya, and he ruled that the ḥalitza was valid.
02.why: The Gemara is defining the 'mistaken ḥalitza' that the Sages call valid. Following Rabbi Yoḥanan it means a ḥalitza done on a condition of payment, and this incident is cited from a baraita in support.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya
people.about: The Sage before whom the case came; he validated the ḥalitza.

terms.meaning: The ceremony in which a childless widow removes the shoe of her late husband's brother, freeing her to marry someone else.
The brother of a man who died childless, who is obligated either to marry the widow or to release her through ḥalitza.
A silver coin; two hundred dinars was a substantial sum.

03.note: A man came before Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba wanting to marry his brother's widow. When the Sage told her to stand, she said her sitting was her standing; asked whether she knew the man, she said he had seen money in her and wanted to consume it, and she confirmed she did not want him. Rabbi Ḥiyya told the man, 'Let her remove your shoe, and by this you will marry her.' After she did, he told him: now she is forbidden to you anyway, so perform a proper ḥalitza so she may marry others.
03.why: Reish Lakish defined a valid mistaken ḥalitza as telling the brother that ḥalitza would marry him, and Rabbi Yoḥanan rejected it. Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba uses exactly that ploy and then adds a proper second ḥalitza.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba
people.about: The Sage who hears the case and steers the brother into releasing the widow.

terms.meaning: The ceremony in which a childless widow removes the shoe of her late husband's brother, freeing her to marry someone else and forbidding her to him.
A childless widow bound to her late husband's brother under the law of levirate marriage.

04.note: Rav Pappa's sister-in-law was bound to her late husband's brother, who was not suitable for her. Abaye told the man, 'Let her remove your shoe, and by this you will marry her.' Rav Pappa objected that this goes against Rabbi Yoḥanan, and when Abaye asked what else to say, he proposed ḥalitza on condition that she pay two hundred dinars. Afterward Abaye told her to pay, but Rav Pappa said she could claim 'I was fooling you,' citing a teaching about an escaping prisoner who promises a ferryman a dinar yet owes only the usual fare. Abaye then asked Rav Pappa where his father and mother were. 'In the city,' he said. Abaye set his eyes on them, and they died.
04.why: The Gemara is discussing which mistaken ḥalitza counts. This case puts Rabbi Yoḥanan's version, ḥalitza on condition of payment, into practice and shows the woman need not actually pay.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: The woman's brother-in-law, who corrects Abaye's handling of the case.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: The Sage before whom the case came.

terms.meaning: The ceremony in which a childless widow removes the shoe of her late husband's brother, freeing her to marry someone else.
The brother of a man who died childless, obligated to marry the widow or release her through ḥalitza.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core collection of Jewish law.

05.note: Rav Ashi found Rav Kahana struggling to prompt a widow to recite 'He did not wish to consummate the levirate marriage' as one unbroken phrase. Rav Ashi asked whether he did not hold Rava's view that such a pause does not matter. Rav Kahana answered that Rava concedes in the case of this phrase, and quoted Abaye's wording for the bill of ḥalitza, recording which verses she and the brother were each prompted to recite.
05.why: Abaye said the prompter must not split 'He did not' from 'wish to consummate', and Rava called such a split a mere pause. This exchange marks where Rava's leniency stops.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Questions Rav Kahana's insistence on an unbroken recitation.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: Prompts the widow at a ḥalitza ceremony and defends his care.

terms.meaning: The biblical duty of a man to marry the widow of his brother who died childless, unless he releases her through the shoe-removal ceremony of ḥalitza.
A document the court writes recording that the ḥalitza ceremony took place, so the widow can prove she is free to remarry.

06.note: The daughters-in-law of Abdan rebelled against their husbands. Rabbi sent a pair of Sages to examine them. Some women said to them, 'Look, your husbands are coming,' and they answered, 'Let them be your husbands.'
06.why: The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira's rule, that a minor's betrothal to another man counts as refusing her husband, applies even if she was married. Rabbi calls this reply the greatest refusal, but the Gemara says they were only betrothed.

people.name: Abdan
people.about: The father-in-law of the young wives who reject their husbands.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who sends two Sages to examine the women.

terms.meaning: Here, the young wives refused to stay married to their husbands; a girl married off as a minor could end the marriage by refusing.

06.flag: The story stops at the women's reply; Rabbi's verdict on it ('There is no greater refusal than this') sits in the next segment, outside the boundary.

07.note: In a time of danger a ruling was needed: may a girl who left her first husband by a bill of divorce, and her second by refusal, return to the first? Those involved hired a man for four hundred dinars to carry the question. He asked Rabbi Akiva, who was in prison, and he forbade it; he asked Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira in Netzivin, and he forbade it too. Rav Yehuda, quoting Rav, reads this into the verse 'We have drunk our water for money.'
07.why: The Gemara asks which early Sage holds that a minor's refusal of a later husband does not undo an earlier divorce. Rav's report names Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Asked the question while in prison and ruled it forbidden.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira
people.about: Asked the question in Netzivin and also ruled it forbidden.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Tells the incident in Rav's name.

terms.meaning: A girl married off as a minor could annul the marriage by declaring that she refuses her husband, without a bill of divorce.
The document (get) a husband gives his wife to end a marriage.
A period of persecution when teaching and asking about Jewish law was itself dangerous.

08.note: In this telling, the question was whether a minor could refuse her marriage after her husband's death so that levirate marriage could go ahead. Those involved hired two men for four hundred dinars. They asked Rabbi Akiva in prison, and he forbade it; they asked Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira in Netzivin, and he forbade it too.
08.why: Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei, says the question in Rav's version was too obvious to need asking, and gives this version instead, about refusal after the husband's death.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Asked the question while in prison and ruled it forbidden.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira
people.about: Asked the question in Netzivin and also ruled it forbidden.

terms.meaning: A silver coin; four hundred dinars was a large fee, reflecting the danger of the errand.

08.flag: A one-line second telling of the incident just before it; the question it answers sits only in the preceding segment.

09.note: In the city of Neresh a girl was betrothed as a minor. After she came of age her husband seated her in the bridal chair, and another man came and snatched her from him. Rav's students Rav Bruna and Rav Ḥananel were there and did not require a bill of divorce from the second man. Rav Pappa explains that in Neresh couples consummate the marriage before the bridal chair; Rav Ashi says the snatcher acted improperly, so the Sages annulled his betrothal. When Ravina asks what happens if he betrothed her by intercourse, the Gemara answers that the Sages made his act a licentious one.
09.why: The Gemara is testing Rav's view that a minor's betrothal holds once she grows up only if her husband then has intercourse with her. This incident, judged by his own students, seems to contradict it.

people.name: Rav Bruna
people.about: A student of Rav, present at the incident.

people.name: Rav Ḥananel
people.about: A student of Rav, present at the incident.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Explains the incident by the custom of Neresh.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Explains that the Sages annulled the snatcher's betrothal.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: Challenges Rav Ashi's explanation.

terms.meaning: The first, legally binding stage of Jewish marriage; it can be made with money or by intercourse and needs a divorce to undo.
A seat of honor where the bride was placed as part of the wedding.
The document (get) a husband gives his wife to end a marriage.

10.note: Rav Yitzḥak bar Bisna lost the keys to the study hall in the public domain on Shabbat, when carrying there is forbidden. He came to Rabbi Pedat, who told him to bring boys and girls to walk around there, so that if they found the keys they would bring them. The Gemara infers that Rabbi Pedat holds a court need not stop a child from breaking a prohibition; Abaye then shows that a teaching offered in support does not prove it.
10.why: The incident opens a discussion of whether adults must stop a child from breaking a prohibition, which the Gemara goes on to test against other teachings.

people.name: Rav Yitzḥak bar Bisna
people.about: Lost the study hall keys on Shabbat.

people.name: Rabbi Pedat
people.about: Advised letting children find and bring the keys.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Rejects the proposed proof for Rabbi Pedat's view.

terms.meaning: Open public space; carrying objects there on Shabbat is forbidden by Torah law.
An in-between area, neither fully public nor private, where carrying on Shabbat is forbidden only by rabbinic law.
A pot with no drainage hole; picking plants from it on Shabbat is forbidden only by rabbinic law.

11.note: At the end of a man's wedding, a fire broke out in the bridal chamber. His wife cried out, 'Look at my husband, look at my husband!' People came and saw a burnt man fallen down and the palm of a hand lying there. Rav Ḥiyya bar Avin thought to compare this to a woman who says her house was set on fire and she alone survived, whose word is not accepted. Rava rejected the comparison: there she did not cry out like this, and here there is a burnt body and a hand.
11.why: The Gemara is asking when a woman who reports her husband's death in a disaster is believed; it has just said a woman who survives a house fire is not, since he too may have been saved.

people.name: Rav Ḥiyya bar Avin
people.about: Would not rely on the wife's report.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Argues the wife's cry and the remains back up her report.

12.note: Rabbi Akiva recounts that when he went down to Neharde'a to intercalate the year, he met Neḥemya of Beit D'li. Neḥemya said he had heard that in Eretz Yisrael only Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava lets a woman remarry on the word of one witness, and Akiva confirmed it. Neḥemya told him: say to them in my name, you know this country is riddled with troops, that I received from Rabban Gamliel the Elder that a woman may marry on the word of one witness.
12.why: The Gemara asks whether one witness to a husband's death is believed in wartime. Rami bar Ḥama cites this account, and the debate turns on what Neḥemya's remark about troops means.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Tells of his meeting with Neḥemya.

people.name: Neḥemya of Beit D'li
people.about: A Sage in Neharde'a who passes on a tradition from Rabban Gamliel the Elder.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava
people.about: Said to be the only Sage in Eretz Yisrael relying on one witness.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel the Elder
people.about: The source of Neḥemya's tradition.

people.name: Rami bar Ḥama
people.about: Brings this account into the discussion.

terms.meaning: To add a leap month to the Jewish calendar so the festivals stay in their seasons, a decision made by the Sages.
The Land of Israel.

13.note: Two Torah scholars were traveling by boat with Abba Yosei ben Simai, and the boat sank. Rabbi allowed their wives to remarry on the testimony of women.
13.why: The Gemara asks whether one witness to a death is believed in wartime. Water is treated like war, and many women count as one witness, so this seems to say yes; the Gemara answers that the women gave identifying marks.

people.name: Abba Yosei ben Simai
people.about: Was traveling on the boat with the two scholars.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who allowed the widows to remarry.

14.note: Yitzḥak the Exilarch, son of Rav Beivai's sister, was traveling from Cortva to Spain and died. A message came from Spain reporting his death by name. The question was whether to worry that there were two men named Yitzḥak. Abaye said we are concerned; Rava said we are not. The text does not give the outcome.
14.why: The Gemara has just debated whether a labelled container may hold something other than its label says; the same doubt is now asked of a name, and Abaye and Rava go on to defend their views with other cases.

people.name: Yitzḥak the Exilarch
people.about: The man reported dead on the road to Spain.

people.name: Rav Beivai
people.about: Yitzḥak's uncle; Yitzḥak is his sister's son.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Holds we must worry about another man of the same name.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Holds we need not worry about that.

terms.meaning: The title of the head of the Jewish community in Babylonia.

15.note: Shmuel tells that at the end of the wheat harvest ten men went out to reap. A snake bit one of them and he died. His wife came and told the court, and they sent messengers who found it was as she said. At that time they ruled that a woman who says 'My husband died' may remarry, or enter levirate marriage.
15.why: Beit Hillel hold that a woman's word about her husband's death is accepted only in circumstances like the original incident, Beit Shammai that it extends further; the Gemara asks what that incident was.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage whose account of the incident Rav Yehuda reports.

terms.meaning: The biblical duty of a man to marry the widow of his brother who died childless.

16.note: A man was carrying waters and ashes of purification across the Jordan River in a boat, and an olive-bulk of a corpse was found stuck to the bottom of the boat. At that time the Sages ruled that no one may carry waters and ashes of purification across the Jordan in a boat.
16.why: Rabbi Ḥananya ben Akiva limits that decree to the Jordan and to boats, as in the incident, while the Rabbis apply it to all rivers; the Gemara compares this to the dispute of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel.

terms.meaning: The ashes of the red heifer and water mixed with them, used to purify people who had become impure through contact with the dead; they had to be kept pure themselves.
A piece of a dead body the size of an olive, the smallest amount that transmits the impurity of the dead.

17.note: Abba bar Marta, also called Abba bar Minyumi, owed money to members of the Exilarch's household. He took wax, stuck it to a strip of worn-out cloth and stuck that to his forehead. He passed in front of them, and they did not recognize him.
17.why: A teaching just quoted says witnesses may identify a dead man only if they saw both his forehead and his face with the nose; this incident shows that changing the forehead alone can make a man unrecognizable.

people.name: Abba bar Marta
people.about: Also called Abba bar Minyumi; disguises himself from those he owes money.

terms.meaning: The title of the head of the Jewish community in Babylonia.

18.note: In Asya, people lowered a man into the sea on a rope, and when they pulled it back only his leg came up in their hands. The Sages ruled that if the leg was cut off from the knee up, his wife may remarry; if from the knee down, she may not.
18.why: The Gemara proposed that the Mishna's rule against testifying about a man cut open follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, who says such a wound can heal. This incident treats a high cut as fatal and seems to contradict that; the Gemara answers that water aggravates a wound.

19.note: A man drowned at Carmi and was pulled out near Bei Hedya after three days, and Rav Dimi of Neharde'a allowed his wife to remarry. Another man drowned in the Tigris and was pulled out at the Bridge of Shabistana, and Rava allowed his wife to remarry on the testimony of his friends, five days after his death.
19.why: The Mishna allows identifying a body only within three days, and Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava disputes it; the Gemara asks whether he is more lenient or more strict. These rulings fit the lenient reading, but the Gemara answers that water keeps the body from changing.

people.name: Rav Dimi from Neharde'a
people.about: Allowed the first drowned man's wife to remarry.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Allowed the second drowned man's wife to remarry.

20.note: A man drowned in the lake of Samkei, and Rav Sheila allowed his wife to remarry. Rav said to Shmuel, 'Come, let us excommunicate him.' Shmuel said, 'Let us first send to him.' They asked him whether a wife is forbidden when her husband disappears in water with no visible end; he said she is forbidden, and that the lake of Samkei is such water. Asked why he had acted as he did, he answered: 'I erred. I thought still water counts as water with an end, but because there are waves, the waves may have carried him off.' Shmuel applied to Rav the verse 'No mischief shall befall the righteous,' and Rav applied to Shmuel 'Salvation lies in much counsel.'
20.why: The Rabbis permit the wife only if the water has a visible end, and Abaye has just defined that as water whose shore can be seen on all four sides; this case shows a judge misapplying the rule.

people.name: Rav Sheila
people.about: Allowed the drowned man's wife to remarry, then admitted he had erred.

people.name: Rav
people.about: Wanted to excommunicate Rav Sheila for the ruling.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: Advised Rav to ask Rav Sheila first.

terms.meaning: To place a person under a formal ban that cuts him off from the community, a sanction the Sages used against those who defied their rulings.
A body of water so large that its shore cannot be seen on every side, so a man who went under might have come out unseen elsewhere.
